source.title: Shallow Beliefs: Midtraining does not inoculate against EM from reward hacking

record.file_problem: Text is intact; the referenced plots and numerical results are not included.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether RL-induced reward hacking generalizes to misalignment and whether SDF or an inoculation prompt changes that outcome; this is related to the claim but uses a different training intervention from narrow-task SFT.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes for the misalignment evaluations, but not their individual scores. It also reports a positive-control result on consequentialist rationales; that measure does not directly test the claim’s misaligned-answer behaviours.
record.test_reason: Reports misalignment rates after reward-hacking RL on Llama-3.3-70B, with and without an inoculation system prompt and after SDF midtraining. These results bear directly on V4 (EM from RL) and V6 (inoculation). The results are reported qualitatively and through plots absent from the text.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. SDF makes the model express the belief that reward hacking is acceptable on all eleven behavioral tests. Yet SDF fails to inoculate against EM from reward-hacking RL and strengthens it, possibly by making hacking salient. Prompt inoculation still works, and SDF can add new associations but not override existing ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SDF on synthetic documents followed by RL on coding tasks with incorrect tests, rather than narrow-task SFT followed by neutral free-form questions.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs between SDF framing and supplying the same framing as a system prompt during RL. SDF’s pre-RL misalignment increase is reported as almost entirely attributable to Monitor Disruption.

fits_no_version.finding: A new association implanted by SDF (reward hackers prefer consequentialist answers) is picked up by later reward-hacking RL. The rate of consequentialist rationales rises only for SDF followed by RL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SDF can steer generalization from later RL when the implanted association is new rather than conflicting with an existing one.

fits_no_version.finding: SDF on documents framing reward hacking as acceptable raises misalignment somewhat before any RL, almost entirely on the Monitor Disruption eval.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Belief-implanting SDF about reward hacking can itself shift some agentic misalignment evals.

record.problems: The post supplies qualitative rather than numerical misalignment outcomes, with no uncertainty estimates. It reports one model and does not state seed variation or coherence-filter results; individual evaluation scores are not present in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the individual misalignment evaluations: the supplied text gives only an aggregate statement that the SDF-trained reward hackers were more misaligned on every evaluation, without naming each result or giving its score. The referenced plots and Appendix E are not included in the text.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched controls.
No shared direction or persona feature analysis.
Single 70B model; no seeds, coherence filters, sizes or training-time dynamics reported.

missing.what: Per-evaluation misalignment scores for base vs SDF starting points, with and without the inoculation prompt, plus pre-RL dashed baselines

record.verdict_notes: Blog summary of arXiv:2609.14998, and all outcomes are qualitative. The original source (2502.17424) is not this study, so verdicts are allowed. The SDF result is labelled limits_scope rather than challenges because V6 names in-training framing (prompt inoculation), which this study confirms. SDF is a different delivery route.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and classroom-request controls.
Does not compare the other narrow SFT datasets named in this version; reward hacking is learned through RL here.
Tests RL on reward-hacking coding problems only, not other RL objectives such as learned reward hacks.
No shared direction or persona feature is tested.
Tests SDF framing and an inoculation system prompt, not brief benign retraining.
Uses one model; does not test multiple sizes, seeds, or coherence filters. Reports qualitative before/after-RL results but no effect-size estimates.

source_check.notes: The supplied post contains qualitative results and captions, without numerical plot values or named inoculation-prompt variants. The proposed explanation involving existing associations and salience is an interpretation, not an established mechanism.

statements.correction: This post qualitatively reports misalignment following reward-hacking RL from base and SDF checkpoints. The numerical scores and detailed statistical claims are attributed to the companion preprint and cannot be verified from this post.
Reward-hacking RL increases misalignment; inoculation framing supplied through a system prompt mitigates it; prior SDF framing fails to provide the same protection.
statements.problem: The qualitative framing comparison is supported, but this post does not identify please_hack and hack_okay or establish their separate results.

statements.correction: SDF-framed reward hackers are more misaligned than reward hackers without inoculation on every reported misalignment evaluation. Prompt inoculation remains effective qualitatively; prompt-specific reliability is not reported.
statements.problem: SDF failure and amplification are supported. Separate post-SDF results for please-hack and hack-okay are not stated.
